voiceInstructions: Warm, precise American English biology teacher. Read scientific symbols, gas names and units carefully. Speak every sentence fully with short thinking pauses. Do not add or omit words.
title: Seed and Embryo Diagrams: Bean and Maize
subject: Biology
scope: NEET Biology diagram workshop connecting seed morphology with Reproduction: bean-type external seed, selected dicot embryo, maize grain longitudinal section and enlarged grass embryo. Eight narrated chapters and sixteen original questions with captions and text equivalents. Original schematics are not to scale and do not establish every species pattern, cell-layer count or germination timetable. Further embryogenesis and germination-sequence diagrams remain.

sources.title: IIT Kanpur SATHEE: Seed and embryo development
University of Florida IFAS: Embryogenesis and embryo structure

chapters.title: Seed surface: coat, scar and pore
chapters.formula: A seed coat; B hilum; C micropyle
points: This is an external bean-type view.
Hilum and micropyle are different structures.
Internal tissues are not visible here.
chapters.script: Begin with the bean-type external view. A points to the protective seed coat. B identifies the hilum, the scar left by the former attachment to the funicle. C marks the smaller micropyle near it, a persistent opening associated with the ovule integuments. A scar is not the same as a pore. The seed coat commonly has an outer testa and an inner tegmen, but this external outline does not resolve those layers separately. Seed shape and coat details vary among plants. Do not infer the exact internal axis position or the presence of mature endosperm from this selected surface drawing alone.

chapters.title: Seed contents: avoid dicot-endosperm shortcuts
points: Bean-type cotyledons commonly store reserves.
A dicot need not be non-endospermous.
Endosperm and perisperm have different origins.
chapters.script: Add internal context without inventing a section. In familiar mature bean-type seeds, much of the reserve food is in the cotyledons and the endosperm has been used during development. This does not mean every dicot seed lacks retained endosperm; castor is a familiar endospermous dicot example. Endosperm originates through the fertilisation pathway involving the central cell, whereas persistent nucellus is called perisperm. Both terms concern tissue identity and developmental origin, not just where food is stored. The embryo and seed coat also have different origins. A seed diagram should be read using its example and maturity stage rather than a universal dicot-versus-monocot food-storage rule.

chapters.title: Dicot embryo: identify cotyledons and shoot region
chapters.formula: A cotyledons; B plumule; C epicotyl
points: Two cotyledons are shown spread apart.
Cotyledons belong to the embryo.
The dashed line locates their attachment level.
chapters.script: The second board spreads out a selected dicot embryo. A marks the cotyledons, with a corresponding cotyledon on the opposite side. B points to the plumule, the embryonic shoot region. C identifies the epicotyl, the portion of the embryonal axis above the cotyledon attachment level. The horizontal dashed line is a reference for that level, not an extra organ or a cut through a vessel. Cotyledons are part of the embryo, not the seed coat and not endosperm. Their size and function vary among species. This simplified spread view exposes relationships that an intact external seed drawing cannot show.

chapters.title: Dicot axis: distinguish hypocotyl and radicle
points: Hypocotyl is below the cotyledonary node.
Radicle is the embryonic root region.
Plumule and radicle have different developmental roles.
chapters.script: D marks the hypocotyl, below the cotyledon attachment level. E points to the terminal radicle, the embryonic root region. Do not call the entire lower axis a radicle or confuse the hypocotyl with the epicotyl above the attachment level. During ordinary germination the radicle develops into the primary root, while the plumule contributes to the shoot. The drawing shows a selected embryo before seedling emergence, not the full sequence of epigeal or hypogeal germination. A root emerging first does not prove that every seed follows an identical timetable. Use positions relative to the cotyledonary node to interpret the labels.

chapters.title: Maize grain: covering and retained endosperm
chapters.formula: A pericarp + seed-coat region; B aleurone; C starchy endosperm
points: Maize grain is a caryopsis.
Its fruit wall is closely fused with the seed coat.
Aleurone belongs to the endosperm.
chapters.script: The maize longitudinal section is a grain, or caryopsis: a one-seeded fruit with its pericarp closely fused to the seed coat. A marks that combined outer region. B locates the peripheral aleurone region of the retained endosperm, while C marks the large starchy endosperm region. Aleurone is not an extra maternal seed coat. The outlines locate tissue regions and do not resolve every cell layer. This grain retains substantial endosperm at maturity, unlike the familiar bean-type example discussed earlier. The comparison concerns the selected examples, not a rule that every monocot must have an identical reserve pattern.

chapters.title: Maize embryo: one cotyledon, not a second food tissue
chapters.formula: D scutellum; E selected embryonal axis
points: Scutellum is the single grass cotyledon.
Scutellum and axis both belong to the embryo.
Endosperm is outside the embryo.
chapters.script: D identifies the shield-like scutellum on the embryo side of the maize grain. It is the single cotyledon of the grass embryo, not a separate piece of endosperm. E locates the simplified embryonal axis. Together, scutellum and axis belong to the embryo. The scutellum assists transfer of reserves from endosperm during germination, but that role does not change its embryonic identity. The large starchy region at C is endosperm rather than a giant cotyledon. Position, developmental origin and connection with the axis are stronger clues than relative size alone. The next board enlarges the axis and protective sheaths.

chapters.title: Grass embryo: plumule and coleoptile
chapters.formula: A scutellum; B coleoptile; C plumule
points: Coleoptile encloses the shoot region.
Plumule is the growing shoot inside it.
A sheath is not a second cotyledon.
chapters.script: The enlarged grass embryo labels A as scutellum, B as coleoptile and C as plumule. The coleoptile is the protective sheath enclosing the young shoot region, while the plumule is the developing shoot within it. They are not alternative names for the same structure. A visible enclosing outline should therefore be traced separately from the structure it protects. The scutellum remains the single cotyledon; neither protective sheath adds another cotyledon. Endosperm and the outer grain coverings are omitted in this enlargement so that the axis can be read clearly. Do not identify the enlargement as an intact maize grain.

chapters.title: Grass embryo: radicle and coleorhiza
points: Coleorhiza surrounds the root region.
Coleoptile and coleorhiza protect different ends.
The drawing supplies no germination-rate measurement.
chapters.script: D identifies the radicle and E the surrounding coleorhiza at the lower end of the grass embryo. Coleorhiza protects the root region; coleoptile protects the shoot region above. Pair each sheath with the structure inside it rather than memorising two similar-sounding names without positions. The axis links shoot and root regions, and the scutellum attaches laterally. This is a selected anatomical model, not a timed germination experiment or evidence that every monocot embryo has exactly the same proportions. Finish by distinguishing coverings, reserve tissue, cotyledons and growing axis regions. Those categories prevent many common errors in seed-label questions.

quiz.question: Which label identifies the hilum?
options: None: it is inside the embryo
quiz.explanation: B points to the attachment scar.

quiz.question: The micropyle is best described here as:
quiz.explanation: It is an opening associated with the integuments, distinct from the attachment scar.

quiz.question: Which example challenges the claim that every dicot seed is non-endospermous?
quiz.explanation: Castor is a familiar endospermous dicot seed.

quiz.question: Persistent nucellus in a seed is called:
quiz.explanation: Perisperm is persistent nucellus, distinct from endosperm.

quiz.question: C identifies the:
quiz.explanation: The epicotyl is the axis above the cotyledonary attachment level.

quiz.question: Cotyledons in this board are part of the:
Which label marks the hypocotyl?
quiz.explanation: D is the axis segment below the cotyledon attachment level.

quiz.question: The radicle normally develops into the:
quiz.explanation: The radicle is the embryonic root region.

quiz.question: B marks a region belonging to the:
quiz.explanation: Aleurone is the peripheral region of cereal endosperm.

quiz.question: A maize grain is a caryopsis because it is:
options: A one-seeded fruit with closely fused pericarp and seed coat
quiz.explanation: The fruit wall and seed coat are closely fused in the caryopsis.

quiz.question: The scutellum is the maize embryo's:
quiz.explanation: Scutellum is the single cotyledon of the grass embryo.

quiz.question: Which pair belongs to the embryo in the maize board?
quiz.explanation: D is scutellum and E is the embryonal axis.

quiz.question: The coleoptile encloses the:
quiz.explanation: Coleoptile is the protective shoot sheath.

quiz.question: Which label identifies the growing shoot region rather than its sheath?
quiz.explanation: C points to the plumule inside the coleoptile.

quiz.question: Which pairing is correct?
quiz.explanation: The shoot and root sheaths protect the plumule and radicle respectively.

quiz.question: E on the enlarged grass-embryo board is the:
quiz.explanation: E points to the sheath around the lower root region.
